Name: The King's Arms
Address: 45 West Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1BU
Description: Grade II-listed timber-framed inn on West Street, billed as Dorking’s oldest pub, with oak-beamed ceilings, leaded windows and four levels of cosy alcoves in what began as three cottages.
History: Historic England dates the timber frame to the early 16th century and earlier. The pub itself says it was built in 1405 and is Dorking’s oldest building, but the listing doesn’t confirm that date. Dorking Museum calls it the town’s oldest remaining pub, open as an inn by 1724, with parts of the building from the 14th century. Reportedly it became a coaching inn in the 16th century. Local tradition says King Charles II once stayed here. The pub also says Charles Dickens wrote about it in Little Dorrit, though no passage naming it has been identified.
Food_and_Drink: Shepherd Neame ales, including Spitfire and Bishops Finger, plus wines, bar snacks, mains and desserts. Food is served most days.
Atmosphere: Traditional characterful pub with real fires and two courtyard gardens, the larger one with an outdoor TV for sport. Live music on Saturdays from 9pm, acoustic Sunday sessions and regular quiz nights.

Name: The Queen's Head
Address: 1 Horsham Road, Dorking, Surrey RH4 2JS
Description: Historic former coaching inn dating from the 1780s, with a tile-hung mansard roof and a large terraced garden.
History: Reportedly built as a private home before becoming a coaching inn in the 19th century, and said to have hosted Victorian ‘smoking concerts’. The pub says it is named after Queen Anne.
Food_and_Drink: Seasonal British food with a focus on quality ingredients. Fuller’s London Pride on cask. Closed on Mondays.
Atmosphere: Cosy historic pub with a real fire in winter and a large terraced garden with tipi dining. Dogs on a lead are welcome in the bar, garden and tipi.

Name: The White Horse
Address: High Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1BE
Description: Grade II-listed coaching inn on the High Street, with a large bar, a restaurant and 56 rooms after a £4 million refurbishment that reopened it in February 2024.
History: There has been a building on the site since at least 1278, when the Knights Hospitaller owned the ‘Cross House’ here. Most of today’s building is 18th century, with parts from the 15th and 16th centuries. It thrived in the coaching era, and from 1823 to 1848 its keeper was William Penn, a descendant of the founder of Pennsylvania. Local tradition holds that Charles Dickens stayed here while writing The Pickwick Papers. A visit by Jane Austen is only rumoured, and even the hotel calls it a rumour.
Food_and_Drink: Seasonal menu, Sunday roasts, steak nights, a children’s menu and a dog menu. Food is served all day.
Atmosphere: Elegant refurbished historic inn with a courtyard, fires and a mix of bar and dining areas, run by Heartwood Inns. Dog-friendly, with dog-friendly rooms. Central location.

Name: The Old House at Home
Address: 24 West Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1BY
Description: Timber-framed building with parts dating to the 14th or 15th century, originally four cottages. Cosy pub with wood panelling and a unique ‘Narnia’ room entered through a wardrobe.
History: Converted into an inn in the mid-1800s by carpenter and beer seller Francis Turner, who had renamed it the Old House at Home by 1855. It was renamed the Old House in 2013. Dorking Brewery took on the lease in October 2023 and restored the old name after a refurbishment in 2024.
Food_and_Drink: Dorking Brewery cask and keg beers plus guest ales. Home-made food, including Sunday roasts.
Atmosphere: Characterful timber-framed interior with fires, wood panelling, the Narnia room and a patio garden with beach-hut style seating. Live music on Fridays. Dog-friendly.

Name: The Bull's Head
Address: 11 South Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 2DY
Description: Old tile-hung former coaching inn on Pump Corner, up a few steps from South Street, with plenty of wood panelling inside.
History: Opened in the 1700s. Dorking’s poultry market, famous for the five-toed Dorking chicken, was once held outside. The inn was the base for two stagecoach firms. Dickens’ Tony Weller in The Pickwick Papers is thought to be based on one of their proprietors, William ‘Old Hold Hard’ Broad, whose London coaches left here at 7 every morning. He was not the landlord, as is sometimes said.
Food_and_Drink: Weekly-changing real ales, often including Otter, St Austell or Timothy Taylor, plus cocktails all day.
Atmosphere: Classic town pub with live music on Saturdays and a couple of tables outside by the side door.

Name: The White Hart
Address: 5 Dene Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 2DR
Description: Small, lively drinkers’ pub just off the High Street, known locally as ‘the Snakepit’, with cellars cut into Dorking’s sandstone caves.
History: A long-established Dorking inn. An old advert on the wall gives sale details from 1849, describing a good bar, tap room, parlour and ‘a well of fine spring water’. One of the cave cellars can still be seen behind a gate at the back.
Food_and_Drink: Surrey Hills Shere Drop on cask. No food is served, but you can bring your own if you ask first.
Atmosphere: Lively local with a horseshoe bar, pool table, big-screen sport and a jukebox. The gents is entered through a police telephone box, like the Tardis.

Name: The Star
Address: 36 West Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1BU
Description: Small, slate-hung historic town pub on West Street, with pavement tables that catch the evening sun.
History: Dates from the early 19th century. It was a Friary Meux pub until it was sold to Greene King in 1990.
Food_and_Drink: Usually three Greene King-supplied ales, sometimes from a local brewery. No food, but you can bring your own or have it delivered.
Atmosphere: Music-led local with vinyl night on Wednesdays, when customers bring records, open mic on Thursdays, and bands or DJs at weekends. Board games and books. Dog-friendly, with biscuits and a water bowl.

Name: The Spotted Dog
Address: 42 South Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 2HQ
Description: Recently refurbished town-centre local on South Street with two large bow windows and a garden looking towards Denbies and Ranmore Common.
History: A traditional South Street local, recorded as trading at 42–43 South Street by Dorking Museum.
Food_and_Drink: Pub food and drinks. Real ale is sometimes available.
Atmosphere: Community local with Sky Sports, live bands and solo artists, DJ nights and a quiz. Family-friendly garden with play equipment. Dogs on a lead are welcome.

Name: The Surrey Yeoman
Address: 220-222 High Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1QR
Description: Tile-hung town pub at the top of the High Street, with beams and a mix of carpet, tiles and floorboards across several levels.
History: Formerly the Royal Oak. It takes its name from the Earl of Rothes, colonel of the Surrey Yeomanry in the early 19th century.
Food_and_Drink: Home-cooked British pub classics, including steaks, burgers and pasta. Fuller’s London Pride plus a changing cask ale, often from Hepworth.
Atmosphere: Traditional local with a beer garden. Family- and dog-friendly.

Name: The Watermill
Address: Reigate Road, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1NN
Description: Large, food-led pub and restaurant on the Reigate Road, with a garden looking across to Box Hill.
History: Dates from the 1930s. A large single-bar pub with a restaurant at the back.
Food_and_Drink: All-day food from brunch onwards, cocktails and a curated wine list. Three cask ales, including a house Watermill ale brewed by Greene King and local guests from breweries such as Dorking, Pilgrim or Surrey Hills.
Atmosphere: Newly renovated interiors with log fires, candlelit tables and a side and rear patio garden. Happy hour on Thursday and Friday, 4 to 7pm.

Name: The Cricketers
Address: 81 South Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 2JU
Description: Small, traditional Fuller’s pub on South Street with bare-brick walls covered in old photos and a lovely walled Georgian garden.
History: A long-standing Dorking local. Etched glass on the old exterior doors shows it once had several separate bars.
Food_and_Drink: Fuller’s ales, including London Pride and ESB, plus Dark Star Hophead and a guest. Pizzas, chips and basket snacks.
Atmosphere: Classic local with darts and board games, rugby and big matches on TV, live music on the last Friday of the month and a monthly quiz. Dog-friendly, with treats at the bar.

Name: The Lincoln Arms
Address: Station Approach, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1TF
Description: Classic Victorian station hotel beside Dorking’s main station, now a relaxed pub with 18 en-suite rooms.
History: Built in the railway age as the Star & Garter. It was later the Happy Days Hotel before becoming the Lincoln Arms.
Food_and_Drink: Pub food and breakfasts. Two or three cask ales, usually including a local one from Dorking, Tillingbourne or Surrey Hills.
Atmosphere: Two large bars, a lounge with pool tables and a quieter wooden-floored back bar with darts, sport on TV and a small paved garden. Handy for both Dorking stations.

Name: Cobbett's
Address: 23 West Street, Dorking, Surrey RH4 1BY
Description: Tiny craft-beer shop and micropub on West Street. Surrey’s first micropub, it’s hidden in a back room called Goldings Bar.
History: Opened as a real-ale off-licence in 2010 in a former doll’s house shop, adding the micropub in July 2014. It is named after the radical writer and farmer William Cobbett, a distant relative of one of the owners.
Food_and_Drink: Cask ales served from the cellar, six keg lines, three draught ciders and a large range of bottled and canned beers. Crisps only, no food.
Atmosphere: Intimate room for about a dozen people, plus a tiny heated courtyard. Closes early, around 8pm most days.

Name: The Falkland Arms
Address: 60 Falkland Road, Dorking, Surrey RH4 3AD
Description: Two-bar community local just south of the town centre, with a sun-trap garden and a decked front terrace.
History: A long-standing traditional Dorking local, listed as trading on Falkland Road by Dorking Museum.
Food_and_Drink: Surrey Hills ales, world lagers, craft beers and cocktails. A short menu of bar snacks.
Atmosphere: Sports pub with TVs in both bars and the garden showing Sky, TNT and Amazon, plus log burners, darts, pool, a jukebox, live music and karaoke, and a fortnightly quiz.

Name: The Dolphin
Address: The Street, Betchworth, Surrey RH3 7DW
Description: Grade II-listed country pub in the heart of Betchworth, opposite St Michael’s Church, in a mid-to-late 18th-century house. The earliest written record of the pub dates from 1785.
History: Local tradition, recounted by Dorking Museum, links the name to the 1216 march of Prince Louis of France, the future Louis VIII, through Betchworth. The ‘Dauphin’ (dolphin) title only came into use in 1349, so it may be a later memory of him. The pub brewed its own beer and cider until 1926, and CAMRA lists its interior as of special national historic interest. Dorking Brewery bought it from Young’s in late 2024, their first freehold pub. The church opposite featured in Four Weddings and a Funeral.
Food_and_Drink: Dorking Brewery cask ales and seasonal pub food.
Atmosphere: Flagstone floors, wood-burning inglenook fires, the old-fashioned Toby Room and a large beer garden. No music or games machines. Dog-friendly, free parking and popular with walkers.

Name: The Running Horses
Address: Old London Road, Mickleham, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6DU
Description: Grade II-listed 18th-century coaching and posting inn on the old London road, an attractive white building with seven en-suite rooms. The pub itself claims more than 400 years as an inn.
History: Named after the 1828 Derby, when Cadland and The Colonel dead-heated and Cadland won the run-off. The sign shows one horse on each side. It reportedly stabled racehorses, and it stands opposite the ancient St Michael’s Church.
Food_and_Drink: Seasonal British menu and bar food, with a sommelier-curated wine list. Real fire in winter.
Atmosphere: Characterful coaching inn with beams, fires, a whisky lounge and a terrace fire pit. Popular with walkers and cyclists. Dogs on a lead are welcome in the bar and on the front patio, but not in the dining room.

Name: King William IV
Address: Byttom Hill, Mickleham, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6EL
Description: Independent family-run free house built in 1790 as an alehouse for workers on the Cherkley Court estate, high on Byttom Hill with panoramic views.
History: Affectionately known as ‘King Bill on the Hill’. It was built for Cherkley estate workers, and Cherkley Court later became the home of press baron Lord Beaverbrook.
Food_and_Drink: Home-cooked traditional pub food served all day, local ales including Dorking and Surrey Hills, Silent Pool Gin and Denbies wines.
Atmosphere: Terraced garden with exceptional views over the Mole Valley and Norbury Park. Real fire, dog-friendly and popular with walkers. Steep access. Open Wednesday to Sunday.

Name: The Stepping Stones
Address: Westhumble Street, Westhumble, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6BS
Description: Country pub named after the famous stepping stones across the River Mole at the foot of Box Hill.
History: Opened in the railway age as the Railway Arms, next to Box Hill & Westhumble station. Now a popular stop for walkers, cyclists and visitors to Box Hill and the North Downs Way.
Food_and_Drink: Seasonal pub food, real ales, wines and local gins.
Atmosphere: Family-, dog- and muddy-boot-friendly, with a beer garden. Monthly jazz club and quiz, plus car and bike club meets. Close to the station, Box Hill and Denbies.

Name: The Inn on the Green
Address: Brockham Green, Brockham, Betchworth, Surrey RH3 7JS
Description: Restaurant-pub in the corner of Brockham’s village green, run as part of the Grumpy Mole group.
History: Formerly the Duke’s Head, reopening as the Inn on the Green in 2010. There has been a pub on the site since at least 1711. The present building dates from about 1900, replacing one that burnt down in 1899.
Food_and_Drink: Food all day, including lunches, afternoon teas and evening meals, and a good wine list. Fuller’s London Pride and Surrey Hills Shere Drop.
Atmosphere: Mostly given over to diners, with a drinkers’ area by the bar, tables overlooking the green and a rear terrace. Popular with walkers.

Name: The Royal Oak
Address: Brockham Green, Brockham, Surrey RH3 7JS
Description: Traditional village pub overlooking Brockham’s picture-postcard green, with Box Hill rising behind and its own resident meerkats.
History: A long-standing village local on the Greensand Way, and a popular stop for walkers.
Food_and_Drink: Good pub food. Fuller’s London Pride and Timothy Taylor Landlord.
Atmosphere: Log-burning stove in winter, a garden with a meerkat retreat and wildlife pond, and a green-side setting.

Name: The Six Bells
Address: Village Street, Newdigate, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5DH
Description: Classic family-run village free house opposite St Peter’s Church, open from 8.30am for coffee and cakes.
History: The pub says it has been here since the 1600s, originally as two cottages. It was formerly the Five Bells and was renamed after the church’s ring was recast as six bells in 1803. The pub gives 1805. Local tradition tells of tunnels linking the pub to the church, smuggling-era lore. The last manorial courts of Cudworth met here in the late 19th century.
Food_and_Drink: Surrey Hills cask ales and a guest, plus coffee, cakes, sausage rolls and scotch eggs from local suppliers. Alcohol is served from 11am.
Atmosphere: Cosy rambling free house with two fires, a large garden with play equipment and a strong community feel. Dogs are welcome throughout.

Name: The White Horse
Address: Shere Lane, Shere, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9HS
Description: Beautiful timber-framed pub in the heart of Shere, built as a farmhouse called Cripps in the mid-to-late 1400s. It became an inn in the late 17th century.
History: A haunt for smugglers in the 18th century. In 1955 a hidden cellar was found containing brandy casks, and renovations also turned up a pair of Elizabethan shoes, traditionally hidden for luck. Local tradition says some timbers came from Nelson’s ship Victory, but this is unproven. The village was a filming location for The Holiday.
Food_and_Drink: Food-focused Chef & Brewer pub with pub classics and seasonal dishes. Greene King and local ales. Real fire.
Atmosphere: Multi-room historic interior on several levels, with beams and a sheltered garden. Well-behaved dogs are welcome in the bar area, where you order through the app, but not in the restaurant.

Name: The Wotton Hatch
Address: Guildford Road, Wotton, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6QQ
Description: Large roadside country pub and restaurant on the A25, with a garden overlooking the North Downs. About 300 years old.
History: Formerly a Surrey Trust Company house, it later belonged to Fuller’s and then Bass. It is now run by Mitchells & Butlers. It sits close to the Wotton estate, birthplace of the diarist John Evelyn.
Food_and_Drink: Gastro-pub style food served all day, real ales including St Austell Tribute, and two real fires.
Atmosphere: Large bar areas, a conservatory and an extensive garden with North Downs views. Dog-friendly, with parking.

Name: The Plough Inn
Address: Abinger Road, Coldharbour, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6HD
Description: 17th-century former coaching inn in the heart of Coldharbour village, close to Leith Hill, with six rooms, a village shop and a converted barn.
History: A long-standing village inn on an old coaching route from London to the coast, now serving walkers and locals heading to Leith Hill Tower.
Food_and_Drink: Home-cooked seasonal ‘British farmhouse’ food with a French twist, and four handpumps. The pub’s own Leith Hill Brewery, founded in 1996, is listed by CAMRA as closed since February 2024, so its beers may not be on. Check before you go.
Atmosphere: Characterful country pub with a wood-burner, large gardens and a strong walking and cycling connection. The shop serves coffee from 8.30am. Dogs on a lead are welcome.

Name: The Abinger Hatch
Address: Abinger Lane, Abinger Common, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6HZ
Description: Pretty wisteria-clad 17th-century village pub in Abinger Common, opposite St James’s Church, family-owned and run since 2017.
History: A former Surrey Trust Company house. The rambling interior covers three levels with flagstones, bare boards, beams and an English oak bar.
Food_and_Drink: Seasonal à la carte menus with plenty of gluten-free, dairy-free and vegan options. Surrey Hills ales and craft keg beers. The kitchen is open all day.
Atmosphere: Two log fires, an extensive garden with a tipi that’s heated in winter, and summer BBQs. Family- and dog-friendly throughout.

Name: The Bray
Address: Shere Lane, Shere, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9HS
Description: Food-led village pub at the top of Shere, still signed The William Bray, with terrace views across the Surrey Hills. Under new ownership since May 2025.
History: Built in the late 18th century as Cook’s Beer House, with an early 20th-century frontage. As the Prince of Wales it was supplied by the Reffell brewery of Gomshall and later Young’s. Former Formula One driver Julian Bailey renamed it the William Bray in 2009. The name comes from the Bray family, lords of the manor of Shere since 1487, whose William Bray (1736–1832) was the noted historian of Surrey.
Food_and_Drink: Breakfast pastries and coffee from 10am, then lunch and supper daily from seasonal, locally sourced menus. Local ales including Surrey Hills Shere Drop, fine wines, weekend cocktails and G&Ts.
Atmosphere: Bar with a wood-burner, a conservatory, a restaurant and an outdoor terrace with views. Dogs are welcome everywhere except the restaurant.

Name: The Royal Oak
Address: The Glade, Felday Road, Holmbury St Mary, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6PF
Description: 17th-century village pub beside the church and green in Holmbury St Mary, run by local residents since February 2023.
History: A centuries-old inn that keeps many original features. The Felday Brewery next door closed in late 2024.
Food_and_Drink: Home-made food, craft beers and local ales, including Firebird, Harvey’s and Surrey Hills. Kitchen hours vary seasonally.
Atmosphere: Cosy bar with a fire, front and back gardens with an outside bar, and a lockable cycle rack. Dog-friendly, with water and treats. Popular with walkers and cyclists.

Name: The King's Head
Address: Pitland Street, Holmbury St Mary, Dorking, Surrey RH5 6NP
Description: 17th-century free house tucked up a back lane at the foot of Holmbury Hill, recently refurbished, with three en-suite rooms and a village shop.
History: The pub once brewed its own beer and was later a Friary Meux house until 1979. It is now locally owned.
Food_and_Drink: À la carte menu using seasonal produce, including veg from its own walled kitchen garden, with roasts on Sundays. Real ales from local breweries. The shop serves coffee from 8am.
Atmosphere: Traditional country bar with a fireplace between two bars, a glass-walled rear extension and a landscaped beer garden. Dog-friendly and popular with walkers and cyclists.

Name: The Hurtwood Inn
Address: Walking Bottom, Peaslake, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9RR
Description: Family-run bar, restaurant and boutique hotel in the heart of Peaslake, a hub for Hurtwood walkers and mountain bikers.
History: Built in 1920 and long the hub of village life. Owned since 2019 by Matt Morris, who had a career in Formula 1, and his family. The rooms are now run as the separate Hurtwood Hotel.
Food_and_Drink: Home-cooked English and Italian food. Surrey Hills Shere Drop, Timothy Taylor Landlord, local craft beers and world wines.
Atmosphere: Bright contemporary bar with a modern inglenook. Well-behaved dogs are welcome in the bar. Cyclists and hikers welcome.

Name: The Surrey Oaks
Address: Parkgate Road, Parkgate, Newdigate, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5DZ
Description: Country free house outside Newdigate in a building dating partly from the 16th century, now under new family ownership.
History: Began life as a wheelwright’s cottage and became a pub around 1850.
Food_and_Drink: Three cask ales, around six ciders and a dozen craft keg beers. Food in the Georgian restaurant.
Atmosphere: Low-beamed flagstone bar with an inglenook and wood-burner, plus several smaller rooms and a very large garden with three boules pistes and a children’s play area.

Name: The Prince of Wales
Address: Guildford Road, Westcott, Dorking, Surrey RH4 3QE
Description: Relaxed village pub and restaurant on the A25 in Westcott, with a bar, garden and separate function room.
History: A local village inn just west of Dorking.
Food_and_Drink: Restaurant open Wednesday to Sunday for lunch and dinner, including Sunday roasts, plus a bar menu. Usually two cask ales, often Timothy Taylor Landlord.
Atmosphere: L-shaped wooden-floored bar full of natural light, a back dining room with a wood-burner, tables out front and a garden below the road. Bar open daily.

Name: Gomshall Mill
Address: 52 Station Road, Gomshall, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9LB
Description: Pub and restaurant inside a 17th-century timber-framed watermill spanning the River Tillingbourne, with the restored water wheel turning in the dining room.
History: A mill at Gomshall is recorded in the Domesday Book, valued at 3s 2d. The present building was a flour mill. A 1950s millstone is set into one of the floors.
Food_and_Drink: Food-focused, with three or four mostly local ales, including Hogs Back TEA. Monthly ribs night.
Atmosphere: Dining areas over several levels around the wheel, with the stream racing beneath, a wood-burner and a riverside garden. Monthly quiz, live music twice a month and an annual duck race.

Name: The Royal Oak
Address: Chart Lane South, Stonebridge, North Holmwood, Dorking, Surrey RH5 4DJ
Description: Traditional country pub overlooking open fields between Dorking and North Holmwood, now under new ownership.
History: CAMRA dates parts of the building to 1613. The pub says it has traded since the mid-18th century and has seen the rise and fall of the nearby Dorking Brickworks, now North Holmwood Nature Reserve.
Food_and_Drink: Traditional home-made pub food, occasionally local game, with Sunday lunch. Guest ales from Dorking Brewery.
Atmosphere: Low-ceilinged split-level restaurant, a main bar and a garden with heated patios. Walks start from the door, including the Deepdene Trail. Dogs on a lead are welcome in the bar.

Name: The Compasses Inn
Address: 50 Station Road, Gomshall, Surrey GU5 9LA
Description: Riverside free house on the A25 at Gomshall, with the Tillingbourne running between the pub and its beer garden, which you reach over a little bridge.
History: CAMRA dates the pub to 1830, and the pub says it was first registered in 1829 to serve beer to local farmers. It is a former Surrey Trust Company house. The pub says it was first called ‘God Encompasses’, which was so often misheard as ‘Goat and Compasses’ that the name stuck, before ‘Goat’ was dropped. Local tradition tells of a friendly ghost, a young woman said to have drowned in the Tillingbourne while escaping a fire at the pub, who reportedly turns on the taps and skips across the water.
Food_and_Drink: Surrey Hills Brewery ales, including Shere Drop. Home-made food cooked to order from bar snacks to full meals, with a specials board and smaller portions. Breakfast is served from 9am to 11am, but alcohol is only sold from midday.
Atmosphere: Separate bar and restaurant with a wood-burning stove, and a riverside garden. The pub says it is dog friendly.

Name: The William IV
Address: Little London, Albury, Guildford, Surrey GU5 9DG
Description: Grade II-listed country pub down a quiet lane at Little London on Albury Heath, with beams, flagstones and a big open fire, surrounded by woods that are popular with walkers.
History: Historic England lists it as an early 16th-century timber-framed building, refronted and extended in the 19th century, with an open fireplace that still has its salt niche and the wooden slots for a cooking crane. The Albury History Society’s building survey puts the original two-bay timber-framed house in the late 15th century. The pub was extensively refurbished in 2024.
Food_and_Drink: Local ales such as Harvey’s Sussex Best, Surrey Hills Shere Drop and Timothy Taylor Landlord. Ingredient-led food from an open grill and wood-fired oven, much of it sourced within 10 miles, with a pizza oven fired up Thursday to Sunday. Closed on Mondays.
Atmosphere: Two traditional bars and a dining room up a few steps, with a winter wood fire. Outside seating, half of it under a canopy.

Name: The Parrot Inn
Address: Horsham Road, Forest Green, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5RZ
Description: Large Brunning & Price pub on the east side of Forest Green, overlooking the green and its cricket pitch, with flagstones, an inglenook and big gardens.
History: A former Surrey Trust Company house. The pub’s own history cites a record of 1712 in which John Evelyn of Wotton agreed a lease with Walter Miall of Abinger for a cottage on ‘Farlyes Green’, as Forest Green was then known. CAMRA says the name is thought to come from smuggling, and local historian Kathy Atherton notes anecdotal 19th-century accounts linking the inn to smuggling, including attacks on excise officers there. The pub itself admits the origin of the name is a mystery.
Food_and_Drink: Brunning & Price menus of classic British dishes with wider influences, updated daily, plus local ales. Coeliac UK accredited. Sunday roasts.
Atmosphere: Several beamed rooms with floorboards, rugs and armchairs, with one end kept for dining. Large gardens with picnic tables, many under a big teepee. A monthly pub walk sets off on the first Saturday of each month.

Name: The Scarlett Arms
Address: Walliswood Green Road, Walliswood, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5RD
Description: Grade II-listed Badger pub in the hamlet of Walliswood, a classic country local with stone-flagged floors, oak beams and an inglenook fire.
History: Historic England describes a 17th-century timber-framed building, later clad in whitewashed brick and extended to the rear in the 19th century. The pub and CAMRA say it was built as two cottages in 1620 and became a pub in 1907. It is named after Sir James Scarlett, the first Baron Abinger, who was Attorney General and Lord Chief Baron of the Exchequer.
Food_and_Drink: Hall & Woodhouse (Badger) ales, including Badger Best Bitter and Fursty Ferret, plus a seasonal Badger guest. Lunch from Wednesday to Sunday and dinner every day except Sunday.
Atmosphere: Several cosy rooms with open fires and stoves, and a darts board. A large garden with a children’s play area. The pub says dogs and bicycles are welcome.

Name: The Cricketers Arms
Address: Stane Street, Ockley, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5TP
Description: Grade II-listed village free house on the old Roman road through Ockley, with a huge inglenook fireplace, flagstones and beams.
History: Historic England dates the building to the late 16th and 17th centuries, with 19th- and 20th-century extensions, under a roof of Horsham stone slabs. The pub says it dates back to the 15th century and was a coaching inn on Stane Street, the Roman road from London to Chichester. The pub also says the actor Oliver Reed was a frequent visitor.
Food_and_Drink: Harvey’s Sussex Best and Surrey Hills Shere Drop, with an occasional guest. Food is limited to Friday evening and Sunday lunch, with occasional pop-up evenings, so check before you go.
Atmosphere: Traditional, unfussy village local with a wood burner in the inglenook. A Sunday afternoon meat raffle raises money for the air ambulance. Closing times vary with custom, so ring ahead if coming from a distance.

Name: The Crown
Address: 98 The Street, Capel, Dorking, Surrey RH5 5JY
Description: Grade II-listed village pub beside Capel churchyard, set back from The Street behind an old timber-and-brick front, with a big garden and play area.
History: Historic England dates it to the late 17th century, with 20th-century extensions to the rear, and notes that one gable once bore the date 1687 and the initials WS. The Victoria County History of 1911 says the inn was originally a farmhouse. CAMRA describes it as 16th century, but the listing doesn’t confirm that.
Food_and_Drink: Two changing guest ales, often from Dorking, Surrey Hills or Hogs Back breweries. Burgers, local pork pies and sausage rolls, a specials board and a Sunday roast. Closed on Mondays.
Atmosphere: Wooden-floored front bar with TVs for sport, a small lounge and a restaurant extension. A large garden with a children’s play area.

Name: The Pheasant at Buckland
Address: Reigate Road, Buckland, Betchworth, Surrey RH3 7BG
Description: Big, comfortable Brunning & Price dining pub on the A25 at Buckland, with garden-room dining, open fires and a terrace looking out over the countryside.
History: The pub’s history says it began as ‘The Tap’ in the late 18th century, next door in what is now Jolly Farmers Cottage, where bricks are stamped 1766. It was ‘The Tap House’ in the 1846 tithe survey, was bought by Reigate’s Mellersh & Neale brewery in 1899, and became the Jolly Farmers, which had moved into the present building by the 1930s. Brunning & Price reopened it as The Pheasant in December 2015. Local tradition tells of the Buckland Shag, a monstrous horse said to haunt the nearby Shag Brook. The pub says the parson had the Shag Stone removed in 1757.
Food_and_Drink: Brunning & Price menus updated daily, with Harvey’s Sussex Best, Surrey Hills Shere Drop and other local ales, and a large gin collection.
Atmosphere: Bustling central bar, a light garden room and comfy seats by open fires. A sunny terrace with an outdoor fire. CAMRA says dogs on a lead are welcome in the bar.

Name: The Red Lion
Address: Old Road, Betchworth, Surrey RH3 7DS
Description: Family-run country inn on Old Road, Betchworth, overlooking its own cricket ground, with ten en-suite rooms and a party room built into the old cellars.
History: The pub says it was built in 1759, and CAMRA says parts date from the 16th century, with the round wooden barn underneath the pub being the oldest part. The wisteria over the pergola is reportedly more than 230 years old. The cricket pitch is home to Reigate Pilgrims Cricket Club, who play there on summer Sundays.
Food_and_Drink: Home-made food made fresh to order, from countryside classics to seasonal dishes, served all day. Three changing ales, usually including at least one local beer.
Atmosphere: Family-friendly pub set in 18 acres, with a large garden, a pergola and marquees for events. CAMRA calls it very dog friendly, and pets can stay in the rooms for a fee.
